opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my first reaction was a mix of excitement and a little bit of shock. Before that, most of my mental model of AI products was the chat box: you ask a question, the model answers, and the interaction ends there. When I first set it up and let it actually run on my own machine, connected to my files, my messaging apps, my calendar, it felt completely different. It wasn't waiting for me to ask something. It was more like having someone sitting at a computer on my behalf.

What struck me most was how simple the design philosophy was. It didn't try to build a fancy interface or a lot of specialized features. It basically gave the model a computer, memory, and access to the tools you already use, and then trusted the model to figure out the rest. That made me realize something about product design in this era: when the underlying model gets strong enough, the best product is sometimes the one that gets out of the way. A lot of the value comes from giving the model the right environment and permissions, not from wrapping it in layers of hand-designed workflows.

At the same time, I noticed the rough edges right away. It would sometimes do things I didn't expect, or take a long, roundabout path to finish a simple task. And there's a real question of trust when something has that much access. So my takeaway was twofold. First, the agent form factor is clearly where things are heading, because people want something that actually gets work done, not just something that talks. Second, the bottleneck has shifted. It's less about whether the model can answer correctly, and more about whether it can plan over long horizons, recover from mistakes, and act reliably in a messy real-world environment. That experience made me think much more seriously about what kind of capabilities we should be training models for.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, my first time using it was a bit of a shock, and not in the way I expected.

I came in with the mindset of someone who had spent years building models. So I was prepared to judge it on benchmarks, on how smart it felt, on whether it could handle the hard coding tasks I threw at it. And it did reasonably well on those. But that wasn't what stayed with me.

What stayed with me was how little it asked of me. I gave it a messy, half-formed description of a problem in a codebase I barely remembered, and instead of demanding that I clarify everything upfront, it went and looked. It read files, ran things, came back with a plan, and told me where it was uncertain. The intelligence was almost hidden behind the workflow.

That reframed how I think about product design for these systems. We tend to think the model is the product. It's not. The model is more like an engine, and the product is the entire loop around it: how it gathers context, when it decides to act versus ask, how it reports back, how it recovers when something goes wrong. A slightly weaker model inside a very well-designed loop beats a stronger model inside a clumsy one, at least for daily work.

The second thing I noticed was restraint. There's a temptation when you build an agent to make it do as much as possible, to show off. OpenClaude felt like it had been designed by people who had been burned by that. It would stop before doing something irreversible. It would tell me plainly when a test failed instead of smoothing it over. That kind of honesty is a design decision, not a model capability, and it builds trust faster than any demo.

So if I had to summarize, that first session taught me that the real design question isn't "how capable is this?" It's "how does it behave when the user isn't watching every step?" That's a much harder problem, and I think it's where most of the interesting work is now.

astra-6.text: What stood out to me was how much product design matters beyond the model itself. As a user, you don’t experience a model in isolation—you experience how you ask a question, how the response is presented, and how easily you can take the next step. That first experience made me think about whether the product helps people express what they want and stay in control. For me, that’s a useful way to judge an AI product: not just whether it gives an impressive answer, but whether it makes the whole interaction easier.
